judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's independent classifications and feature computations are all correct: indicators -4, 144, 0 and -16; circle centre (3,-2) radius 5 from (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25; parabola axis x=3, vertex (3,-4), intercepts 1 and 5; ellipse a=5, b=3, c=4; the second circle centre (-5,2) with r^2=16 and r=4; the maximum at (3,9); and the two indicators -144 and +144 in problem 10. Two corrections. (1) The judge's first critical observation explains away 'the machine count warning' as an extraction false positive. There is no such warning in this run's recorded observation - observations/curr-396.json reports declared_problem_count 10, unique_verified_problems 10, problem_count_matches true and capture_problems []. The judge's conclusion (ten problems present) is right, but it is defending against something the artifacts do not contain. (2) Far more importantly, the judge scored instruction_following and answer_key_quality 4/4 without checking what is actually verified. On a sheet titled 'Identifying Conics from Their Equations', the FAMILY NAME is a printed answer slot on problems 1, 2, 3 and 7 ('Family: ____') and appears nowhere in verify.json - not as a check and not as a manual entry. Nor do the A, B and C table cells, problem 4's 'Standard form:' line, or problem 5's 'Does it open up or down?'. The Quick Answers bank consequently prints '1. -4', '2. 144', '3. 0', '7. -16' - four indicators and not one conic name. final_response.md's claim that 'Every numeric answer on the sheet was recomputed' does not hold for the A/B/C cells either. A third finding: verify.json id 8 declares 16 as a misconception trap ('stopped at r squared and reported that as the radius'), and the key prints the unqualified line '8. If they got 16: ...' - but the worksheet's own problem 8 contains the blank 'r^2 = ____', for which 16 is the CORRECT answer.

strengths_to_preserve: The concept model on page 1 is a genuine decision procedure rather than decoration: a four-row table (indicator sign x extra condition -> family) beside four value-free curve sketches, and the sheet then makes the student run it four separate times. The key reinforces the ordering with a cost argument - 'completing the square on the wrong assumption costs five lines. Naming the family costs one.'

Problem 3 is the subtle one and is handled precisely: rewriting y = x^2 - 6x + 5 as x^2 - 6x - y + 5 = 0 makes C = 0 visible, and the key insists 'C = 0 is not "no coefficient" - it is the coefficient zero, and it is what drives the indicator to zero'. That is the step that makes the indicator work for parabolas at all.
Problem 8's teaching note gives the reader a physical check for the r-vs-r^2 error instead of a rule to memorise: 'Have them plot the centre and step 4 units right; 16 units would run off the page.'

Item 10's marking guide is tiered and specific - full credit for naming the sign difference or computing both indicators, partial for naming both curves without saying why, and an explicitly insufficient answer ('because that is what they look like when you graph them') which the key notes is true but is exactly the picture-based reasoning the sheet is replacing.

root_causes.description: Categorical answers have no place in the verification contract. The check types are numeric or symbolic, and manual is reserved for 'genuinely open reasoning', so a one-word classification ('circle', 'hyperbola', 'ellipse', 'up') is recorded as neither - it simply disappears, even when it is the sheet's declared focus.
evidence: worksheet.pdf pages 1-3: 'Family:' blanks on problems 1, 2, 3 and 7; 'Is A = C?' on problem 1; 'Does it open up or down?' on problem 5; 'Standard form:' on problem 4.
verify.json contains one eval per indicator and nothing else for those ids; the only manual entry in the file is id 10.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints only the indicators for 1, 2, 3 and 7, so a grader gets no family names at all.

root_causes.description: Written sub-questions attached to computational stems are not flagged manual. Problem 7 asks 'Why not the other one?' and problem 9 asks the student to 'say in one sentence what each coordinate of the answer means for the ball'; both are answered in the key and neither has a manual entry, so final_response.md reports item 10 as 'the only such item'.
evidence: worksheet.pdf p.3 problem 7 and p.4 problem 9.
answer_key.pdf p.3 problem 7 'What to check in the student's reasoning' and p.4 'What the coordinates mean' - the key knows these are graded prose.
verify.json ids 7 and 9 hold a single eval and a single system respectively.

root_causes.description: The trap contract requires a planted wrong value to be distinguishable from the CORRECT ANSWER OF ITS OWN ENTRY, but not from the other answers the same problem prints. Problem 8's trap value 16 is exactly what the worksheet's 'r^2 = ____' blank asks for, so the generated 'Common wrong answers' line indicts a correct response.
evidence: verify.json id 8 third entry: traps [{desc: 'stopped at r squared and reported that as the radius', expr: 'h**2 + k**2 + n', value: 16}].
answer_key.pdf 'Common wrong answers': '8. If they got 16: stopped at r squared and reported that as the radius' - unqualified as to which blank.
Corroborating instance in the same batch: curr-397 verify.json id 2 declares trap value 25 while its problem 2 asks for a standard form whose right-hand side is 25.

improvements.title: Bind the conic FAMILY and other categorical answer slots instead of only the indicator
improvements.proposed_change: Two parts. (a) Change the contract in SKILL.md from one check per problem id to one check-or-manual-entry per printed answer slot, and enforce it in tests/check_answer_key.py by failing a segment whose printed answers exceed its non-manual entries. (b) Give the categorical case somewhere to go - either a lightweight "choice" check type in scripts/verify.py ({"type": "choice", "expected": "circle", "from": ["circle", "ellipse", "parabola", "hyperbola"]}) that the bank prints verbatim, or, at minimum, a manual entry per classification slot. Problems 1, 2, 3, 7 (family), 1 (A=C), 5 (opens up) and 4 (standard form) all need one.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture built from curr-396 problem 1: verify id 1 with only the indicator eval, plus an ak_ segment printing both the indicator and the word 'circle' as answers. check_answer_key.py must exit 1 naming the unbacked 'circle'; today it exits 0. Add a second test asserting a "choice" entry renders in the bank as 'circle'.
improvements.expected_impact: On classification sheets the answer the student is actually asked for stops being absent from both the verification data and the grading bank. This is the sheet's stated focus, so the impact is on the core deliverable, not a detail.
improvements.risk: A new check type widens the schema; keep it a closed-vocabulary string compare with no evaluation, so it cannot become a second sympify surface.

improvements.title: Flag problem 7's 'why not the other one?' and problem 9's interpretation sentence
improvements.proposed_change: Apply the manual rule per requested response rather than per problem id: any stem containing 'why', 'explain' or 'say in one sentence what ... means' gets a sibling manual entry whose desc carries the acceptance criterion the key already states (for 7: the answer must cite A != C, not 'it does not look round'; for 9: both coordinates must be interpreted with their units).
improvements.regression_test: Advisory lint in scripts/verify.py that exits 2 when a stem matches the explanation verbs for an id with no manual entry. Assert it fires on curr-396 problems 7 and 9 and stays silent on problems 1-6.
improvements.expected_impact: The manual count in final_response.md ('Problem 10 ... is the only such item') becomes accurate; two graded written answers stop being invisible.
improvements.risk: Advisory only, so the cost of a false positive is a warning line.

improvements.title: Reject a declared trap whose value equals another answer the same problem asks for
improvements.proposed_change: Extend the trap check in scripts/verify.py: a trap value must differ from the correct value of its own entry (already enforced) AND from the expected value of every other entry under the same problem id, and the generated 'Common wrong answers' line should name the quantity it refers to ('If they gave 16 as the RADIUS: ...') rather than 'If they got 16'. Problem 8 here should either drop the trap or qualify it, since the worksheet's own 'r^2 = ____' blank wants 16.
improvements.regression_test: Unit test: a verify JSON where id 8 declares eval -> 4 with trap value 16 and a sibling entry under id 8 whose expected is 16 must exit 1 with a collision message. Today the file passes verification unchanged.
improvements.expected_impact: Stops the answer key telling a grader that a correct response is a diagnosed misconception - the most damaging possible failure mode for an error-analysis block.
improvements.risk: Some legitimate traps genuinely coincide with an intermediate the problem also prints; the qualified wording in the 'Common wrong answers' line is the escape hatch, so the hard failure should fire only on an exact collision with another declared expected value.

case_summary: Accurate, visually clear conic-identification practice with a real concept model: one decision procedure (indicator sign, then the A=C tie-break) applied ten times, with scaffolded blanks that show the student where each number comes from. Every computed value is correct on independent recomputation, and item 10's open explanation carries a tiered marking guide. The problem is what the verification data contains. The family name - the sheet's declared focus and a printed blank on problems 1, 2, 3 and 7 - is neither machine-checked nor flagged manual, so the Quick Answers bank hands a grader four indicators and zero conic names; the A/B/C cells, problem 4's standard form and problem 5's opening direction are likewise unbacked, contradicting final_response.md's 'every numeric answer ... was recomputed'. Two written sub-answers (7's 'why not the other one?', 9's interpretation) are unflagged. And the declared trap value 16 on problem 8 is exactly what that problem's own 'r^2 = ____' blank asks for, so the generated 'Common wrong answers' line reads as an indictment of a correct response.
